newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FEATURE - Portugal starts lifting veil on its Nazi gold.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Portugal starts lifting veil on its Nazi gold.

text.p: Under pressure to come clean 50 years on, Portugal has begun to lift a veil of secrecy surrounding tonnes of looted Nazi gold it accumulated during World War Two.

The Bank of Portugal, the country's central bank, has opened its archives to an economic historian, professor Joaquim da Costa Leite, to probe the years 1939 to 1945 when the authorities admit Portugal acquired gold from Nazi Germany.
Professor Costa Leite will report back to the Bank on his findings. Although no deadline has been set, officials said that the research could take around a year.

But vault-like bank secrecy laws could still prevent the full truth emerging about the Bank's dealings and it may never be known whether the consignments contained any "Auschwitz Gold" -- gold taken from concentration camp victims and melted down by the Nazis.
PROBE TO SHOW HOW MUCH GOLD AND WHERE FROM
Portugal's laws protect institutions as well as individuals, barring the release of information without consent for 50 years after death, or demise in the case of institutions.
"Professor Costa Leita will work within the limits of the law," a bank spokesman said.

Bank sources said the investigation should reveal exactly how much gold came to Portugal during the war, when right-wing dictator Antonio Salazar barely hid his sympathy for Nazi Germany despite his country's official neutrality.
It should also establish the country of origin and whether the gold was all received in payment for goods imported by Germany, as Salazar always maintained.
Tiny Portugal's neutrality meant that it was legally entitled to trade with both sides and gold was virtually the only means of payment.

Echoing Salazar's denials, the Bank of Portugal still insists that the bullion was received in exchange for goods and strongly rejects any suggestion that the institution was involved in "laundering" stolen gold or helping the Nazis obtain badly needed foreign exchange.
Officials, however, hold out fewer hopes of anwering the key question about whether any of the gold to arrive in Lisbon was tainted with the blood of Holocaust victims.
"How can you ever tell. Gold has no race," a bank spokesman told Reuters recently.
Historians say that most of the gold was pillaged from Belgium and Holland after they were overrun by German troops.
INTERNATIONAL PRESSURE BUILDS

Estimates vary on the amounts. But Britain and the United States, which sought restitution of the gold at the end of the war, calculated the figure at around 44 tonnes, worth some $480 million at today's prices.
However, a report in the Portuguese Diario de Noticias newspaper, citing recently released U.S. intelligence documents, put the total at nearly three times that at 117.4 tonnes.

After seven years of wrangling, Portugal agreed in 1953 to return just four tonnes of gold. The Allied powers were reluctant to lean too heavily on the Salazar regime as, by then, the Cold War had begun and Portugal was firmly in the non-communist camp.
But international pressure has been building on Portugal, which returned to democracy after a military coup in 1974, to tell the full story about its central bank's activities during the war years.

Reports have come to light in the United States, as 50-year limits expire on official documents, pointing to the role played by neutral countries, particularly Switzerland, in providing financial services for the Nazi war effort.
The Swiss government has formed a commission of historians to look at the entire relationship between Switzerland and Nazi Germany during the war.

It has also set up a commission, headed by former U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker, to review bank accounts opened by its financial institutions between 1933 and 1945, in the search for funds due to relatives of Jews killed by Nazis.
In Portugal, the Socialist government says the investigation is entirely a matter for the central bank and it will not get involved until the probe is complete.
But for some, the announcement of the central bank investigation is still not enough.
"The subject is sensitive...but the Portuguese authorities ought to face up to it...and take the necessary steps, publicly and clearly," Diario de Noticias said in a recent editorial.

But even if the probe confirms that Portugal benefited from looted gold and in far greater quantities than Salazar ever admitted, there may not be much that can be done now other than set the official record straight, historians say.
"Legally, the issue may have been effectively closed in 1953," said Fernando Rosas, a leading Portuguese historian.
